issues.legal_issue: A person who did not make a false document cannot be convicted of forgery merely because they caused another person to make it or benefited from its use.
material_facts: An impersonator posed as the property owner and executed a power of attorney in favour of one accused.
The accused later used the power of attorney in a mortgage transaction, but the courts made no finding that either accused made the false power of attorney or any part of it.
The evidence identified the impersonator, rather than either accused, as the person who executed the power of attorney.
issues.conclusion: A forgery conviction requires proof that the accused made the false document; the accused could not be convicted as its maker merely because one benefited from the transaction or executed the later mortgage deed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 463 and 464 IPC must be read together: Section 463 defines forgery, and Section 464 identifies when a false document is made. Section 465 punishment requires proof of forgery under Section 463, including the making of a false document under Section 464. Applying strict construction of penal statutes, the Court held that making a document differs from causing it to be made. It relied on Dickins v. Gill, (1896) 2 QB 310; Md. Ibrahim v. State of Bihar, (2009) 8 SCC 751; and Mir Nagvi Askari v. Central Bureau of Investigation, (2009) 15 SCC 643.

predicates.forgery_prosecution: The proceeding seeks to establish that an accused committed forgery.
predicates.accused_not_proved_to_be_maker_of_false_: The prosecution has not proved that the accused made the false document or any part of it.

issues.definition: When a forgery prosecution does not prove that the accused made the false document, the accused cannot be convicted of forgery on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A forgery conviction cannot stand where the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the case rests on suspicion or the accused’s benefit from the transaction.
material_facts: The impersonator who executed the power of attorney was not found or investigated.

Forensic evidence showed that the signature and fingerprints on the power of attorney did not match those of the property owner, but the prosecution did not prove that either accused made the document.
The trial and appellate courts relied on the accused’s benefit from, or involvement in, the mortgage transaction, without proof that they made the false power of attorney.
The High Court acquitted the accused, and the complainant appealed that acquittal.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove the forgery charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: In a criminal trial, guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; strong suspicion, coincidence, or grave doubt cannot replace proof. A reasonable doubt must be practical rather than an abstract theoretical hypothesis. The Court relied on Latesh @ Dadu Baburao Karlekar v. State of Maharashtra, (2018) 3 SCC 66, and applied the principle that penal liability cannot be established by inference from benefit or suspicion alone.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_acquittal and prosecution_did_not_prove_accused_made_false_document and imposter_not_investigated and conviction_rested_on_suspicion_or_benefit

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_did_not_prove_accused_made_f: The prosecution did not prove that the accused made the false document.
predicates.imposter_not_investigated: The person who impersonated the true document-maker was not located or investigated.
predicates.conviction_rested_on_suspicion_or_benefi: The conviction relied on suspicion or the accused’s benefit from the transaction rather than proof of the charged conduct.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal against an acquittal, where the prosecution did not prove that the accused made the false document, the impersonator was not investigated, and the conviction rested on suspicion or benefit, the acquittal is upheld because guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
